title: Book of Acts IQ
subtitle: How well do you know the early church's first chapters?

questions.text: Who wrote the book of Acts?

options.explanation: Acts opens by referring back to a "former treatise," the Gospel of Luke. Both are addressed to Theophilus, and the author is traditionally Luke, the physician who traveled with Paul.
Peter is a major figure in the first half of Acts, but he didn't write it.
Paul dominates the second half of the story, yet the narrator writes about him in the third person, then later joins as a traveling companion.
John appears alongside Peter early on, but he is not the author.

questions.text: What happened to the believers on the Day of Pentecost?

options.text: They were baptized in the Jordan River
options.explanation: John the Baptist baptized in the Jordan, but Pentecost was a different event entirely.

options.text: The Holy Spirit came on them with wind and tongues of fire
options.explanation: Acts 2 describes a sound like a rushing wind, tongues like fire resting on each person, and the believers speaking in other languages so the crowd could understand.

options.text: They saw Jesus ascend into heaven
options.explanation: The ascension happens in Acts 1, before Pentecost.

options.text: They chose a replacement for Judas
options.explanation: Matthias was chosen in Acts 1, just before Pentecost.

questions.text: Who was chosen to replace Judas among the twelve apostles?

options.explanation: Barnabas was an encourager and a missionary partner of Paul, but he was not the one chosen here.
Stephen was one of the seven chosen to serve tables, and later the first martyr, but not Judas's replacement.
In Acts 1:26, the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
Silas became a companion of Paul later in the book, not a replacement for Judas.

questions.text: Who was the first Christian martyr, stoned to death after preaching boldly?

options.explanation: James the brother of John was put to death by Herod in Acts 12, but that came after the first martyrdom.
Acts 7 records Stephen's long sermon and his stoning. As he died he asked the Lord not to hold the sin against them.
Philip the evangelist kept ministering, including to the Ethiopian official. He was not martyred in Acts.
There are two men named Ananias in Acts, but neither was the first martyr.

questions.text: On the road to Damascus, who was struck blind by a bright light and met the risen Jesus?

options.explanation: Cornelius was a Roman centurion who saw a vision of an angel, a different encounter altogether.
In Acts 9, Saul was traveling to arrest believers when a light flashed and a voice said, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" He was blinded for three days.
Apollos was an eloquent teacher from Alexandria, not the man on the Damascus road.
Timothy joined Paul's missionary work later and is never described having this experience.

questions.text: Who was the first Gentile convert, a centurion visited by Peter?

options.explanation: The Ethiopian official was reached by Philip, not Peter, and he was already a worshiper of God on his way home.
Lydia was a seller of purple in Philippi, reached later through Paul's ministry.
Acts 10 tells of Cornelius, a devout centurion in Caesarea. Peter visited him, and the Holy Spirit fell on his household, opening the door to the Gentiles.
The jailer believed after the earthquake in Acts 16, but Cornelius came first.

questions.text: In which city were the disciples first called Christians?

options.explanation: Jerusalem was the birthplace of the church, but the name Christian started elsewhere.
Acts 11:26 says the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch, where Barnabas and Saul taught for a whole year.
Rome is where the book ends with Paul under house arrest, but the name began earlier.
Ephesus saw a powerful ministry from Paul, but it was not where the name first appeared.

questions.text: Who were Paul's main companions on his first missionary journey?

options.explanation: Acts 13 sends out Barnabas and Saul, with John Mark as their helper. John Mark later turned back, which became a point of tension.
Peter and John ministered together in Jerusalem and Samaria, not on Paul's first journey.
Silas and Timothy joined Paul on later journeys, after the split with Barnabas.
Luke and Aquila were part of Paul's wider circle, but not the first-journey team.

questions.text: What happened to Paul and Silas in the Philippian jail at midnight?

options.text: An angel carried them out the gate
options.explanation: That was Peter's rescue in Acts 12, a separate jailbreak.

options.text: They escaped through a window in a basket
options.explanation: Being lowered in a basket happened to Saul over the wall of Damascus, not to Paul and Silas in Philippi.

options.text: They sang hymns, and an earthquake shook the doors open
options.explanation: Acts 16 says they were praying and singing when an earthquake struck, the doors opened, and the chains came loose. The jailer and his household then believed.

options.text: They were released the next morning with an apology
options.explanation: An apology did come later when the officials learned Paul was a Roman citizen, but the dramatic moment was the midnight earthquake.

questions.text: In Athens, where did Paul preach his famous sermon about the "unknown god"?

options.explanation: The temple of Diana was in Ephesus, where a riot broke out over Paul's preaching.

options.text: The Areopagus, also called Mars' Hill
options.explanation: Acts 17 places Paul on the Areopagus, where he pointed to an altar inscribed to an unknown god and proclaimed the God who made the world.
Solomon's porch was at the temple in Jerusalem, the setting for earlier preaching.
The Bereans searched the Scriptures daily, but that was a different stop before Athens.

questions.text: How does the book of Acts end?

options.explanation: Acts does not record Paul's death. Tradition places it later, but the book closes before that.

options.text: With Paul preaching freely in Rome under house arrest
options.explanation: Acts 28 ends with Paul in Rome, welcoming all who came to him and preaching the kingdom of God with boldness, no one forbidding him.
The second coming is promised in Acts 1, but the book itself ends with Paul in Rome.

options.text: With the conversion of the emperor
options.explanation: No emperor is converted in Acts. The book ends with Paul still preaching while waiting for trial.

scoring.perfectMessage: You know the early church inside and out!
